rule: Audit trail is always on for every GMP-relevant create, modify, delete, sign, status change and configuration change (MBR design, library blocks, master data, roles, limits, execution data, review/release). No tenant, site, MBR, role or administrator setting can disable, pause, filter at capture time, edit or purge it.
why: Audit trail is the evidence that records were not altered without trace; if it could be configured off, no configuration of the product could be trusted. The Annex 11 revision concept paper explicitly says it should not be possible to deactivate audit trail functionality or edit its data.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 11.10(e); EU GMP Annex 11 section 9 (and 2025 draft section 12); FDA Data Integrity Q&A (2018)

rule: Original values are never overwritten or deleted. A correction creates a new value version linked to the original, with who/when/why (reason mandatory), and the original stays visible in the record and in review views; 'delete' of GMP data is replaced by invalidation with reason.
why: Part 11 requires that record changes not obscure previously recorded information; EU Chapter 4 requires alterations to be signed, dated and to leave the original readable, with a reason where appropriate; Annex 11 requires the reason for change or deletion of GMP data to be documented.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 11.10(e); EU GMP Chapter 4 (alterations to entries); EU GMP Annex 11 section 9

rule: All GMP timestamps come from a synchronised, server-side trusted time source (stored in UTC with the site's offset); client device clocks and user-typed dates are never used as the time of an action. User-entered event times (e.g. 'time the autoclave cycle started' from a printout) are stored as data fields distinct from the system timestamp of entry.
why: Audit trails must be computer-generated and time-stamped and signatures must carry date and time; contemporaneity and sequence checks (hold times, time limits) are meaningless if the clock can be manipulated from the client.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 11.10(e), 11.50(a)(2); EU GMP Annex 11 sections 9 and 14; 21 CFR 211.111

rule: Every electronic signature shows the signer's printed name, the date/time and the meaning of signing (e.g. performed, verified, reviewed, approved, released), and is cryptographically bound to the exact content signed (e.g. hash of the step result and its context) so it cannot be removed, copied or transferred to another record; any later change to signed content invalidates or supersedes the signature visibly.
why: Signature manifestation and signature/record linking are explicit Part 11 requirements; Annex 11 requires e-signatures to be permanently linked to their record and to include time and date.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 11.50, 11.70; EU GMP Annex 11 section 14

rule: Signing requires at least two distinct identification components (user ID + password) or a biometric; the first signing in a continuous controlled session uses all components and later signings at least the private component; signings outside a continuous session re-use all components. Configuration may make this stricter (e.g. always full re-authentication, MFA), never weaker; no 'remember my signature' or pre-signing.
why: Minimum e-signature component rules are regulatory; weaker settings would make every signature in every configured MBR non-compliant.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 11.200(a), 11.300; EU GMP Annex 11 section 14

rule: Only unique, individually assigned user accounts can perform GMP actions; shared, generic or service accounts cannot sign, execute steps or approve. Accounts are never deleted or reassigned to another person (disable only), so historical attribution survives.
why: Attributability; FDA discourages shared logins because actions cannot be traced to a person; e-signatures must be unique to one individual and not reused or reassigned.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 11.100(a), 11.10(d); FDA Data Integrity Q&A (2018); EU GMP Annex 11 section 12

rule: Authority checks are evaluated by the engine at the moment of each action: the user must hold a role permitted for that action on that step type/MBR/site AND (where configured as a prerequisite) have current training on the governing document/MBR version; failing checks block the action rather than warn.
why: Part 11 requires authority checks so that only authorised individuals can sign, alter records or perform the operation; 211.25 requires personnel to have training for their assigned functions.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 11.10(g), 11.10(i); 21 CFR 211.25; EU GMP Chapter 2; Annex 11 section 12

rule: For any step configured with a verification (second-person check/witness), the verifier must be a different authenticated individual from the performer (and from any other signer that the step's segregation rule excludes); the engine rejects same-user verification regardless of role or admin rights. Manual component charge-in and manual yield calculation always carry mandatory independent verification; the only permitted reduction to single-person verification is when the operation itself was performed by qualified automated equipment and one person checks that it did so correctly.
why: 211.101(d) and 211.103 require a second person for manual charge-in and yield calculations and 211.68(c) allows automated equipment to substitute for the performer only; 211.188(b) requires identification of persons performing and checking each significant step. A verifier identical to the performer is no verification at all.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.101(c)-(d), 211.103, 211.68(c), 211.188(b)(11); EU GMP Chapter 4 (batch processing record: initials of operator and, where appropriate, of the person checking)

rule: MBR (master record) lifecycle is fixed: authored by one person, independently checked by a second person, and approved by the quality unit before it can become effective; author, checker and QA approver must be distinct users; approval signatures cannot be configured away (no 'skip review' switch for GMP masters). Customers may ADD reviewers/approvers to the route, not remove the minimum.
why: 211.186(a) requires the master record to be prepared and signed by one person and independently checked and signed by a second; 211.100(a) and 211.22 require quality unit approval of production procedures and changes to them. A vendor option to bypass review for testing must be confined to non-GMP use.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.186(a), 211.100(a), 211.22(c); EU GMP Chapter 4 (approval of manufacturing formula and processing instructions)

rule: A GMP batch record can only be issued from an MBR version in Effective status, for a product/site/batch size within that version's approved scope; the issued record is an exact, hash-verified instantiation of that version (plus batch-specific header values). Later MBR edits never change records already issued; retiring or superseding an MBR is a new controlled version, not an in-place edit.
why: The batch record must be an accurate reproduction of the approved master, with transcription error designed out; changes to master records must be instituted only by authorised personnel under control.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.188(a), 211.186, 211.68(b), 211.100(a); EU GMP Chapter 4 (batch processing record based on the approved formula/instructions, method avoiding transcription errors)

rule: The execution engine enforces the step sequence, prerequisites and branch conditions defined in the MBR (operational system checks). A user cannot execute a step whose predecessors are incomplete, re-order steps, or skip a mandatory step; the only way around the defined flow is a documented exception (deviation/unplanned event) approved in the system, which is itself part of the record.
why: Part 11 requires system checks that make the software keep steps and events in their allowed order; 211.100(b) requires procedures to be followed and deviations recorded and justified.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 11.10(f), 211.100(b); EU GMP Chapter 5; EU GMP Chapter 4 (deviations with signed authorisation)

rule: Data are captured contemporaneously: the step result is committed with the server time of entry; the UI offers no way to set an earlier time for the action. Late entries (e.g. recorded after an offline period or after the event) are allowed only as explicitly flagged late entries with reason and are highlighted for review.
why: Procedures must be documented at the time of performance; EU Chapter 4 requires records to be made or completed when each action is taken. Backdating is a classic data integrity failure.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.100(b), 211.188; EU GMP Chapter 4 (records completed at time of action); FDA Data Integrity Q&A (2018)

rule: A value outside its approved limits is always stored exactly as entered or acquired, flagged, and routed to the exception workflow; the operator cannot suppress the flag, and re-entering a new value creates a correction (with reason and the original preserved) rather than replacing the failing result. Whether an exception becomes a formal deviation is a QA decision recorded in the system, never a configuration shortcut.
why: Unexplained discrepancies and failures to meet specifications must be investigated (211.192); deviations must be recorded and justified (211.100(b)); testing into compliance by overwriting is a data integrity violation.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.100(b), 211.192; EU GMP Chapter 1 and Chapter 4 (deviations); FDA Data Integrity Q&A (2018)

rule: Material status and identity are checked by the engine at dispensing and charge-in: only lots in released/approved status, within expiry or retest date, of the item (and grade/supplier where specified) called for by the MBR can be used; quarantined, rejected, expired or blocked lots and wrong items are hard-blocked (no operator override). Identity is confirmed by scanning a system-generated container/lot label, not by typing.
why: Components must be withheld from use until released by the quality unit and used only within retest/expiry; wrong-material and status errors are the main mix-up risk the eBR exists to prevent.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.84(a), 211.87, 211.80, 211.101(a)-(b); EU GMP Chapter 5 (starting materials released by QC; status of materials)

rule: Equipment/room status is checked by the engine before use: the unit must belong to the equipment class required by the MBR, be qualified, within calibration and preventive maintenance due dates, in 'clean' status for the right product/cleaning type and within its clean-hold time, and not in use by another batch; failures block the step. The equipment's unique ID is recorded automatically in the batch record and its logbook.
why: Major equipment identity must be recorded in the batch record; equipment must be cleaned, maintained and calibrated per written programmes and use must be logged.

rule: Batch disposition is blocked while any step is incomplete, any exception or linked deviation is open, required QC/EM results are missing, or required reviews are unsigned. Only users holding the quality-unit disposition role (US) or the Qualified Person role (EU certification) can sign it; the system records who certified/released, and nobody else (including administrators) can set a released status.
why: The quality unit must review and approve production records and investigate discrepancies before release; Annex 11 requires that when a system records certification and release, only QPs can certify and the releasing person is identified; Annex 16 requires the QP to take deviations into account.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.22, 211.165, 211.192; EU GMP Annex 11 section 15; EU GMP Annex 16

rule: Record completeness is enforced: every step of the issued record ends as executed, system-marked not applicable (untaken branch), or not-applicable by an authorised user with reason and signature. Blank or silently skipped steps are impossible at review.
why: Batch records must include complete information about each significant step; blanks are a classic ambiguity and data integrity finding.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.188(b); EU GMP Chapter 4 (batch processing records); FDA Data Integrity Q&A (2018)

rule: GMP records, audit trails and signatures cannot be deleted by any user or configuration during their retention period; retention periods are floors derived from regulation (e.g. US: at least 1 year after batch expiry, longer for certain OTC products; EU: at least 1 year after expiry or 5 years after QP certification, whichever is longer) and legal holds; archived records stay readable (including metadata and audit trail) for the whole period, across system upgrades.
why: Records must be retained and readily retrievable; archiving must preserve accessibility, readability and integrity.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.180(a); 21 CFR 11.10(c); EU GMP Chapter 4 (retention of batch documentation); EU GMP Annex 11 sections 7 and 17

rule: The system can always produce accurate and complete copies of any batch record in human-readable and electronic form, including all values, corrections, exceptions, signatures with their manifestations, attachments and the audit trail, for inspection; export content cannot be trimmed by report configuration below that minimum.
why: Inspectors must be able to review and copy records; printouts must be clear and indicate changed data.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 11.10(b); EU GMP Annex 11 section 8

rule: Configuration layers are separated: MBR/library authors can only compose vendor-defined block types and set their declared options; they cannot alter the engine's enforcement logic. System-level configuration (roles, signature policies, interfaces, rounding policy defaults, numbering) is itself versioned, audit-trailed and changed only via change control, with an exportable, diffable configuration baseline per site/environment.
why: Changes to master records and to the computerised system must be controlled, authorised and documented; configuration drift between validated baseline and production is otherwise undetectable.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.68(b), 211.100(a); EU GMP Annex 11 sections 4 and 10; GAMP 5 2nd ed. configuration management

rule: Customer-defined calculations run only in a sandboxed, deterministic expression language with a closed library of validated functions, compile-time type and unit checking, no loops without bounds, no I/O, no access to other records except declared inputs, and no ability to write data; there is no 'custom script' escape hatch in GMP masters.
why: Formulas embedded in master records must give correct results; an unrestricted scripting facility would turn every MBR into custom (Category 5) software needing code-level verification and would allow logic that bypasses guardrails.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.68(b); EU GMP Annex 11 section 5; FDA Data Integrity Q&A (2018) (MPCR calculations validated); GAMP 5 2nd ed. categories

rule: Critical data entered manually always receives an additional accuracy check (second-person verification, double-blind re-entry, or capture from a validated device instead of typing); the MBR author can choose the method but cannot configure 'no check' for data classed as critical (quantities of materials, CPP values, IPC results, yields).
why: Annex 11 requires an additional accuracy check for critical manually entered data, by a second operator or validated electronic means.
regulatory_basis: EU GMP Annex 11 section 6; 21 CFR 211.101(c), 211.103

rule: MBR approval is blocked by automated completeness/plausibility checks that encode regulatory content minima: e.g. theoretical yield with min/max limits at each yield stage, reconciliation limits for printed labelling, limits on every IPC/CPP field, unit of measure on every quantity, time-limit values with a cited validation reference, required verifications on manual charge-in, and (injectables) PUPSIT/post-use integrity and 100% CCI where applicable unless a QA-approved justification is referenced.
why: The master record has mandatory content; catching omissions statically before approval is cheaper and more reliable than relying on reviewers (PAS-X runs 50+ such checks).
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.186(b), 211.125(c), 211.111; EU GMP Chapter 4; EU GMP Annex 1 (2022) sections 8.22 and 8.87

rule: Test, simulation and training executions are technically segregated from GMP execution: they run only on masters in Draft/Test status or in a non-production mode, their records are watermarked, excluded from inventory/equipment/genealogy updates in production, and can never be converted into or merged with GMP batch records; conversely a GMP record can only come from an Effective master.
why: MBR verification by test runs is essential, but test data leaking into GMP records (or unapproved masters producing GMP records) would break record integrity.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.100(a), 211.186; EU GMP Annex 11 sections 4 and 10; FDA Data Integrity Q&A (2018)

rule: The review-by-exception report is generated by the engine from a mandatory exception taxonomy (limit breaches, overrides, corrections, late entries, interface fallbacks, time-limit breaches, open verifications, unplanned interventions, alarm events classed critical, audit-trail events on critical data). Customers may add exception types or raise severities but cannot remove mandatory types or hide events from review.
why: Review by exception is only acceptable if the system provably surfaces everything a full review would find; audit trails of critical data must be reviewed before the record is approved.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.192; EU GMP Annex 11 section 9 (audit trail review) and draft (2025) section 12; FDA Data Integrity Q&A (2018)

rule: System administrators (IT/configuration roles) cannot execute, verify, review or release GMP steps, cannot change GMP data values, and cannot grant themselves GMP roles without a second approver; all privileged actions are audit-trailed. Password/lockout/session-timeout policies have regulatory floors that configuration can tighten but not loosen.
why: Segregation of duties and access controls prevent undetected manipulation; Annex 11 expects access restricted to authorised persons and changes to access recorded; Part 11 requires controls over ID codes/passwords.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 11.10(d), 11.10(g), 11.300; EU GMP Annex 11 section 12; FDA Data Integrity Q&A (2018) (restricting admin rights)

rule: Data acquired from instruments, scales, PLC/DCS, BMS/EMS or LIMS keep their provenance (source, device ID, source timestamp, raw value, unit) and the interface verifies completeness/accuracy of transfer; when an interface is bypassed, the value is marked as manually transcribed and requires verification.
why: Electronic data exchange with other systems must include built-in checks for correct and secure entry; input/output of computer systems must be checked for accuracy.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.68(b); EU GMP Annex 11 section 5

rule: Every executed step stores the effective versions and actual values of all master data it used (specification limits, equipment status, material status, MBR/library version, SOP version, calculation version). Later master data changes never alter what an executed record shows or how its results were evaluated.
why: Records must reflect what was actually done under the instructions and limits in force at the time; retroactive changes through master data would silently rewrite history.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.188, 11.10(e); EU GMP Chapter 4; EU GMP Annex 11 section 10

rule: If offline or edge execution is supported, offline entries are signed and hashed locally with a trusted, synchronised clock, uploaded in order, never overwrite server data on conflict (conflicts become exceptions), and are flagged as offline-captured for review; signature rules and status checks that need server data are either pre-cached with validity windows or block the step.
why: Network outages must not create gaps in attributability, contemporaneity or sequence enforcement.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 11.10(e)-(f); EU GMP Annex 11 sections 5, 9 and 16 (business continuity)

rule: Stored values are language- and locale-neutral (canonical number, unit code, UTC time); language, decimal separators and date formats affect display only. Translations of MBR text are approved as part of the MBR version and a language switch can never change a limit, unit or instruction meaning.
why: Multi-language sites must not create divergent instructions or mis-parsed numbers (decimal comma vs point) in the GMP record.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.100(a), 211.186; EU GMP Chapter 4 (clear, unambiguous documents)

rule: The electronic record is the master; any printout is marked as a copy with print time, printer user and record status, and wet-ink signatures on printouts never substitute for the electronic signatures required by the MBR. Hybrid (paper) steps are allowed only as MBR-defined, controlled forms that are issued, reconciled and scanned back as certified true copies.
why: Hybrid situations are a frequent source of ambiguity about which record is authoritative; FDA and the Annex 11 draft address hybrid records and true copies explicitly.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 11.70; EU GMP Annex 11 section 8 and draft (2025) section 13 on hybrid solutions; FDA Data Integrity Q&A (2018)

rule: (Injectables edition) A sterile batch cannot be dispositioned unless its sterility-assurance evidence chain is complete and reviewed: passing sterilisation/depyrogenation records for all product-contact items and their hold times, passing post-use filter integrity (and PUPSIT unless QA-justified), EM and personnel monitoring results for all sessions, the filling line and all aseptic operators holding valid APS/gowning qualification on the fill date, all interventions reviewed, 100% visual inspection and CCI results, and sterility/endotoxin results (or authorised parametric release).
why: Sterility cannot be tested into a batch; Annex 1 and the FDA aseptic guidance expect these records to be reviewed as part of batch release.
regulatory_basis: EU GMP Annex 1 (2022) chapters 7-10; 21 CFR 211.113(b), 211.167(a), 211.192; FDA Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing guidance (2004) batch record review section

rule: (Tablets edition) Periodic IPC failures or missed checks during compression, coating or packaging automatically put the output produced since the last passing check on hold at container level (containers are time-stamped and IDs recorded), so the affected quantity is traceable and cannot be merged with good output before QA disposition.
why: In-process controls exist to detect drift during the run; without container-level segregation a failing check cannot be connected to the product it represents.
regulatory_basis: 21 CFR 211.110(a)-(c), 211.192; EU GMP Chapter 5
